title: Heating of black-Si by microwaves at 2.45 GHz: effect of nano-needle orientation
authors: Massimiliano Zamengo, Haoran Mu, Hsin-Hui Huang, Tomas Katkus, Darius Gailevičius, Saulius Juodkazis, Junko Morikawa
abstract: Silicon, which is highly reflective and has negligible absorption at the microwave 2.45 GHz range, can be heated when it is turned into black-Si with a surface texture of nano-needles made by SF6/O2 plasma etching. Microwave heating of flat Si and of black-Si with vertical and with tilted (oriented) nano-needles was compared under identical conditions in a cylindrical TM010 resonator. Samples were placed horizontally on a 150-micrometer-thick cover glass, which standardized their height and position inside the cavity and allowed a common calibration of the radiation thermometer against a K-type thermocouple. Under a stepwise protocol of only 2-3-4 W of microwave power (60 s per step), black-Si with vertical needles reached ~ 260 C, systematically exceeding flat Si (~ 190 C), while black-Si with oriented needles showed a delayed but abrupt onset of heating at 3 W. In situ monitoring of the cavity resonance revealed a 2-3 MHz downshift of the resonance frequency f for all samples, with the drift consistently appearing once the sample temperature exceeded ~ 120 - 150 C, consistent with thermally activated carrier generation in Si. At a given temperature, each sample loads the cavity at a different f and quality factor Q, indicating an orientation-dependent effective permittivity of the nano-needle array, in line with the strong form birefringence of tilted black-Si. Application potential and challenges in the quantitative temperature and permittivity determination are discussed.
summary: This paper experimentally investigates microwave heating in black-Silicon structured with nano-needles, comparing vertical and oriented needle arrangements. By monitoring the cavity's resonance frequency and Q-factor as a function of temperature, the authors demonstrate that the needle orientation dictates the effective permittivity and the material's electromagnetic response to microwave fields.
main_problem: The study investigates how the orientation of nano-needles on silicon surfaces affects microwave heating efficiency and the resulting anisotropic electromagnetic response when irradiated at 2.45 GHz.
main_result: The nano-needle texture significantly enhances microwave absorption, leading to higher heating rates compared to flat silicon, and the resonance frequency and quality factor show strong dependence on needle orientation and temperature.
method: Microwave heating experiments were conducted in a cylindrical resonator, monitoring the resonant frequency and quality factor in situ while varying microwave power and measuring temperature with a radiation pyrometer.
model_or_system: The system involves black-Si samples (flat, vertical, or oriented nano-needles) placed in a microwave cavity at 2.45 GHz. The physics is governed by the temperature-dependent, anisotropic effective permittivity ($\epsilon_{	ext{eff}}$) of the structured material.
key_observables: Resonance frequency ($f$), Quality factor ($Q$), surface temperature ($T$), and effective permittivity ($\epsilon_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Microwave frequency (2.45 GHz), microwave power (2-4 W), and temperature range ($\sim 190^\circ	ext{C}$ to $260^\circ	ext{C}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the measured frequency/Q-factor shifts are dominated by changes in the effective permittivity due to temperature-activated carrier generation and dielectric polarization.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, time evolution of temperature and resonance parameters ($f$ and $Q$) for different needle orientations, and plots showing the sample-specific frequency and Q-factor dependence on temperature.
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup, compares heating behavior across three sample types (flat, vertical, oriented), and analyzes the temperature-dependent shifts in the cavity resonance parameters to deduce the anisotropic effective permittivity.
why_interesting: The study demonstrates how nanoscale structuring can engineer material properties (like permittivity) in a highly controllable, temperature-dependent manner, which has implications for designing metamaterials or microwave absorbers.

FIG. 2. Schematic of the sample mounting geometry and needle-to-electric field orientation inside the microwave cavity. (a) Sample with vertical b-Si needles mounted horizontally inside the quartz tube; the electric field E is perpendicular to the needles. The diagram shows the pyrometer align- ment spot viewed through the cavity window. (b) Sample with oriented b-Si needles; by rotating the sample, the in-plane projection of the needle axis is set parallel (Case A) or perpendicular (Case B) to E. (c) Cross-sectional view of the quartz tube showing the sample resting on a 150-µm -thick cover glass to ensure consistent positioning at the maximum electric field strength.

FIG. 3. Time evolution of the surface temperature during the 2-3-4 W protocol (60 s per step) for flat Si, b-Si with vertical needles and b-Si with oriented needles (in-plane needle projection parallel and perpendicular to E). Temperature was measured by the calibrated radiation thermometer. b-Si with vertical needles reaches ≈260,◦C at 4 W; the oriented-needle sample heats slowly at 2 W and rises abruptly upon switching to 3 W, overtaking flat Si.

FIG. 4. (a) Resonance frequency f and (b) quality factor Q of the cavity versus time during the heating protocol for the four configurations of Figure 3. f drops by ∼2–3 MHz for all samples; under the 4 W step, Q increases for b-Si with vertical needles while it decreases for flat Si; the oriented-needle sample shows a sudden collapse of Q at the 3 W step followed by a recovery.

Figure 6 gives the overall summary of the experimental results replotted as temperature dependences of the resonance frequency and the Q-factor. Although the f-drift occurs at different times during the power protocol for each sample (Figure 4), when the data are replotted versus the sample temperature the drift consistently appears once the sample reaches approximately 120–150 ◦C, indicating a temperature-activated change in the di- electric properties which is common to all samples. The decrease in resonance frequency indicates that the effective dielectric loading of the cavity increases during heating.
